title: Nahum 3:1–11
context: The prophet cries woe to the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, with no end to the prey. The noise of whip, wheels, horses, and chariots leads into a charge of the slain and of bodies without end, because of the city’s prostitution and witchcraft, by which she sold nations and families. The LORD of Armies says he is against her, and will expose her shame and make her a spectacle, so that those who look will flee and ask who will mourn for Nineveh. The prophet then asks whether she is better than No-Amon, a city situated among the rivers, with waters around her, whose strength was Cush and Egypt and whose helpers were Put and Libya, yet she went into captivity. Nineveh, the word says, will also be drunken, hidden, and seeking a stronghold because of the enemy. Many readers take No-Amon as Thebes in Egypt; the verse describes her situation among the rivers, with a rampart and wall of the sea, and does not use a later place-name.

verses.text: Woe to the bloody city! It is all full of lies and robbery—no end to the prey.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Woe to the bloody city! It is all full of lies and robbery—no end to the prey.” The woe names a bloody city, full of lies and robbery, with no end to the prey. Nineveh is the city in view from the book’s heading and from the naming that will come in verse 7. The charge is blood, deceit, and endless prey, told in that one woe.

Arminian readers hear a moral indictment, a city whose prey has no end, a woe that still treats the blood and the lies as reasons for the judgment, not as fate without a charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the woe, the blood, the lies and robbery, and the endless prey as the LORD’s own opening charge against the city in this last chapter.

Shared ground: the city is bloody, and the prey has no end. The woe is the prophet’s cry over that charge.

verses.text: The noise of the whip, the noise of the rattling of wheels, prancing horses, and bounding chariots,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The noise of the whip, the noise of the rattling of wheels, prancing horses, and bounding chariots,” The line is all sound: whip, wheels, horses, chariots. The sentence runs on into the next verse. The assault is heard before it is seen, and the noise is listed without a longer description.

Arminian readers hear a city already filled with the sound of an attack, a rattling that interrupts the endless prey of the verse before, a word still spoken as warning in the very noises of the streets.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the whip, the wheels, the horses, and the chariots as the sound of the judgment already arriving, the first movement of the scene that follows.

Shared ground: the verse is a list of sounds. The charge of the horseman and the sword comes in the next line.

verses.text: the horseman charging, and the flashing sword, the glittering spear, and a multitude of slain, and a great heap of corpses, and there is no end of the bodies. They stumble on their bodies
verses.arminianNotes:
The sounds become a charge: the horseman, the flashing sword, the glittering spear, and then “a multitude of slain, and a great heap of corpses, and there is no end of the bodies.” They stumble on their bodies. The cost of the bloody city’s way is told in that heap, and the line is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a harvest of the city’s own violence, a multitude of slain with no end of bodies, a word that still names the horror as the fruit of the robbery and prey already charged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the charging horseman, the sword and spear, the multitude of slain, and the heap of corpses as the LORD’s appointed end of the bloody city.

Shared ground: there is no end of the bodies. The verse is sober, and the image is not enlarged.

verses.text: because of the multitude of the prostitution of the alluring prostitute, the mistress of witchcraft, who sells nations through her prostitution, and families through her witchcraft.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason is given: “because of the multitude of the prostitution of the alluring prostitute, the mistress of witchcraft, who sells nations through her prostitution, and families through her witchcraft.” The city is charged as a mistress of prostitution and witchcraft, selling nations and families. The figure names predatory power and deceit, and it is not enlarged.

Arminian readers hear a real selling of nations, a seduction and a sorcery used as tools of empire, and a “because” that still treats the city’s way as the ground of the woe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the prostitution, the witchcraft, and the selling of nations and families as the LORD’s stated reason for the woe and for the exposure that follows.

Shared ground: nations and families were sold through this city’s power. The figure stays in those words, and it is enough.

verses.text: “Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your shame.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your shame.” The LORD of Armies is against her, as in 2:13. The exposure is a public shame before nations and kingdoms, told in the language of a lifted skirt and uncovered nakedness, and it is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a shame equal to the city’s hidden dealings, a showing to the nations she once sold, and an “I am against you” that still addresses her as the one being judged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the “I am against you,” the exposure before the nations, and the showing of shame as the LORD of Armies’ own act, the answer to the hidden prostitution already named.

Shared ground: the LORD of Armies is against her, and her shame will be shown to the nations. The line is sober, and it is not turned into a longer scene.

verses.text: I will throw abominable filth on you and make you vile, and will make you a spectacle.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will throw abominable filth on you and make you vile, and will make you a spectacle.” Filth is thrown, she is made vile, and she becomes a spectacle. The LORD himself does this. The language is of public disgrace, and the filth is named without further color.

Arminian readers hear a making-vile that answers the vileness already charged, a spectacle that the nations will see, a word that still treats the disgrace as the LORD’s moral verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the thrown filth, the making vile, and the spectacle as the LORD’s appointed disgrace of the city.

Shared ground: she will be made a spectacle. The next verse will give the onlookers’ words.

verses.text: It will happen that all those who look at you will flee from you, and say, ‘Nineveh is laid waste! Who will mourn for her?’ Where will I seek comforters for you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
“It will happen that all those who look at you will flee from you, and say, ‘Nineveh is laid waste! Who will mourn for her?’ Where will I seek comforters for you?” Those who look flee, and they say Nineveh is laid waste, and they ask who will mourn. The LORD asks where comforters can be found for her. The name is spoken in the onlookers’ mouth, and the mourning is missing.

Arminian readers hear a loneliness after the spectacle, a waste so complete that no mourner stands forward, a question about comforters that still addresses Nineveh as “you.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the fleeing of the onlookers, the cry that Nineveh is laid waste, the missing mourner, and the search for comforters as the LORD’s appointed isolation of the city.

Shared ground: Nineveh is laid waste, and the question is who will mourn for her. The name is now on the lips of those who flee.

verses.text: Are you better than No-Amon, who was situated among the rivers, who had the waters around her, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was of the sea?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Are you better than No-Amon, who was situated among the rivers, who had the waters around her, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was of the sea?” Nineveh is asked whether she is better than No-Amon, a city set among rivers, with waters around her and a rampart and wall of the sea. Many readers take No-Amon as Thebes in Egypt; the verse itself gives the watery setting and does not use a later place-name. The point of the question is that a well-watered stronghold has already fallen.

Arminian readers hear a comparison Nineveh can still take to heart: a city as guarded by water as she is has already gone down, so her own waters are no proof of safety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the question, the situation of No-Amon among the rivers, and the rampart and wall of the sea as the LORD’s own warning by example.

Shared ground: No-Amon was a water-guarded city, and the question is whether Nineveh is better. The identification with Thebes is a common reading, and the verse does not settle the later name.

verses.text: Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength. Put and Libya were her helpers.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength. Put and Libya were her helpers.” No-Amon’s strength was Cush and Egypt, boundless as it seemed, and Put and Libya were her helpers. The allies are named, and they are the verse’s measure of how strong she looked. The names are given as the WEB gives them, and the line does not map their later histories.

Arminian readers hear a boundless strength that still was not enough, helpers who did not finally keep her, a warning to Nineveh not to trust her own network of power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take Cush and Egypt as boundless strength, and Put and Libya as helpers, as the LORD’s own account of the resources that did not save No-Amon.

Shared ground: her strength and her helpers are named, and they belong to the example already begun. The next verse will say what became of her.

verses.text: Yet was she carried away. She went into captivity. Her young children also were dashed in pieces at the head of all the streets, and they cast lots for her honorable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet was she carried away. She went into captivity. Her young children also were dashed in pieces at the head of all the streets, and they cast lots for her honorable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.” No-Amon went into captivity. Children were killed in the streets, lots were cast for the honorable, and the great were bound. The verse states those losses once, soberly, and they are not described further. Later readers often connect this fall with an Assyrian campaign in the seventh century; the oracle uses the fall as a warning and does not narrate that campaign.

Arminian readers hear a “yet” that overthrows boundless strength, a captivity that came despite rivers and allies, and a warning whose sorrow is named without being lingered over.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the captivity, the death of the children, the lots, and the chains as the LORD’s own reminder of what happened to the city Nineveh is being asked to compare herself with.

Shared ground: she was carried away, and the great were bound in chains. The line is sober, and it is enough.

verses.text: You also will be drunken. You will be hidden. You also will seek a stronghold because of the enemy.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You also will be drunken. You will be hidden. You also will seek a stronghold because of the enemy.” The “You also” turns the example onto Nineveh: she too will be drunken, hidden, and seeking a stronghold because of the enemy. The likeness to No-Amon is now a sentence, not only a question.

Arminian readers hear a “You also” that still addresses Nineveh as one who may take the comparison to heart, a seeking of a stronghold that will not, in this word, be found in time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the drunkenness, the hiding, and the seeking of a stronghold because of the enemy as the LORD’s appointed portion for Nineveh, the “also” of the comparison.

Shared ground: Nineveh too will seek a stronghold because of the enemy. The example of No-Amon has become her sentence.
